nodes.name: Cognitive radio (CR)
nodes.statement: A {\em cognitive radio} (CR) is a frequency-agile wireless communication device with a monitoring interface and intelligent decision-making that enables dynamic spectrum access~\cite{Zhao07c}.
differentia: with a monitoring interface and intelligent decision-making that enables dynamic spectrum access

nodes.name: Channel sensing errors: false alarm and miss detection
nodes.statement: It has been shown in prior work that generally there are two types of channel sensing errors: (i) {\em false alarm}, when an idle channel is identified as busy, thus a spectrum opportunity will be wasted, (ii) {\em miss detection}, when a busy channel is identified as idle, thus leading to collision with primary users, since CR users will attempt to use such ``idle'' channels.
nodes.statement_short: Two sensing-error types: false alarm (idle read as busy, opportunity wasted) and miss detection (busy read as idle, collision with primary users).
differentia: {\em false alarm}, when an idle channel is identified as busy, thus a spectrum opportunity will be wasted
{\em miss detection}, when a busy channel is identified as idle, thus leading to collision with primary users

nodes.name: Network state vector
nodes.statement: We define the {\em network state vector} in slot $t$ as $\vec{S}(t)=[S_1(t),S_2(t),\dots,S_M(t)]$, where $S_m(t)$ denotes the state of channel $m$, for $m=1, 2, \cdots, M$. When channel $m$ is idle, we have $S_m(t)=0$; when channel $m$ is busy, we have $S_m(t)=1$.
differentia: When channel $m$ is idle, we have $S_m(t)=0$
when channel $m$ is busy, we have $S_m(t)=1$

nodes.name: Channel utilization $\eta_m$ and transition probabilities $\lambda_m,\mu_m$
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda_m$ and $\mu_m$ be the transition probability of remaining in state $0$ and the transition probability from state $1$ to $0$ for channel $m$, respectively. Let $\eta_m = \Pr(S_m=1)$ denote the {\em utilization} of channel $m$ with respect to primary user transmissions.
differentia: with respect to primary user transmissions

nodes.name: Time slot structure: sensing phase and transmission phase
nodes.statement: The time slot structure of the proposed MAC protocols is shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:SlotStructure}, which consists of a {\em sensing phase} and a {\em transmission phase}. The sensing phase is further divided into $\bar{K}$ mini-slots, within which each secondary user senses one of the licensed channels. CR users access the channels for data transmission during the transmission phase.
nodes.definiendum: time slot structure of the proposed MAC protocols
differentia: consists of a {\em sensing phase} and a {\em transmission phase}
The sensing phase is further divided into $\bar{K}$ mini-slots
nodes.section: 3 Sensing Error Aware CR MAC Protocol

nodes.name: False alarm probability $\epsilon_m$ and miss detection probability $\delta_m$
nodes.statement: We assume all secondary users have the same probability of detection errors when sensing channel $m$, $m=1, 2, \cdots, M$. Let $\epsilon_m$ and $\delta_m$ denote the probabilities of false alarm and miss detection on channel $m$, respectively. The spectrum sensing performance can be represented by the Receiver Operation Characteristic (ROC) curve, where $(1-\delta_m)$ is plotted as a function of $\epsilon_m$~\cite{Zhao07c}.
nodes.statement_short: Per-channel sensing-error probabilities $\epsilon_m$ (false alarm) and $\delta_m$ (miss detection), identical across users and summarized by the ROC curve.
nodes.genus: probabilities of false alarm and miss detection on channel $m$
differentia: all secondary users have the same probability of detection errors when sensing channel $m$

nodes.name: Conditional channel availability probability $a_{m,k}$
nodes.statement_short: Bayes posterior that channel $m$ is idle given $k$ sensing outcomes, reducing to $(1+\alpha_m^{d_m}\beta_m^{k-d_m}\eta_m/\zeta_m)^{-1}$.
nodes.genus: conditional probability that channel $m$ is available after the $k$th sensing mini-slot
differentia: \Pr(S_m=0 \;|\; W_{m,1}=\theta_{m,1},\cdots,W_{m,k}=\theta_{m,k})

nodes.name: Likelihood ratios $\alpha_m$ and $\beta_m$
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} \alpha_m = \frac{\Pr(W_{m,i}=0 | S_m=1)}{\Pr(W_{m,i}=0 | S_m=0)}=\frac{\delta_m}{1-\epsilon_m}, \; \mbox{for } \theta_{m,i}=0 \\ \beta_m = \frac{\Pr(W_{m,i}=1 | S_m=1)}{\Pr(W_{m,i}=1 | S_m=0)}=\frac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m}, \; \mbox{for } \theta_{m,i}=1. \hspace{-0.05in} \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Per-observation likelihood ratios $\alpha_m=\delta_m/(1-\epsilon_m)$ for a $0$ reading and $\beta_m=(1-\delta_m)/\epsilon_m$ for a $1$ reading.
differentia: \frac{\delta_m}{1-\epsilon_m}, \; \mbox{for } \theta_{m,i}=0
\frac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m}, \; \mbox{for } \theta_{m,i}=1

nodes.name: Stop time $K_m$
nodes.statement: The {\em stop time} $K_m$ when secondary users stop sensing channel $m$, is a random variable that takes value between $1$ and $\bar{K}$, the maximum number of mini-slots that can be used for sensing (see Fig.~\ref{fig:SlotStructure}). If we have $\Theta_0 < a_{m,k} < \Theta_1$ by the end of the sensing phase, then channel $m$ state is not identified due to lack of time (or sensing results) and the channel will not be accessed.
nodes.genus: random variable that takes value between $1$ and $\bar{K}$
differentia: when secondary users stop sensing channel $m$
the maximum number of mini-slots that can be used for sensing

nodes.name: Estimate sets $\Psi^0_{m,k}$, $\Psi^1_{m,k}$, $\Psi^2_{m,k}$
nodes.statement: When there are $k$ sensing results available (e.g., one user senses channel $m$ for $k$ mini-slots, or it senses channel $m$ for less than $k$ mini-slots and receives some channel $m$ sensing results from other secondary users), we define three sets of estimates for the state of channel $m$, as: \begin{eqnarray} \Psi^0_{m,k}&=&\{d_m\;|\;a_{m,k}\le \Theta_0, \forall \; 0 \le d_m \le k\} \\ \Psi^1_{m,k}&=&\{d_m\;|\;a_{m,k}\ge \Theta_1, \forall \; 0 \le d_m \le k\} \\ \Psi^2_{m,k}&=& \{d_m\;|\;\Theta_0 < a_{m,k} < \Theta_1, \forall \; 0 \le d_m \le k\} = \overline{(\Psi^0_{m,k} \cup \Psi^1_{m,k})}, \end{eqnarray} where $d_m$ is the number of observations whose sensing result is $0$ on channel $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Partition the counts $d_m$ of zero-readings into three sets according to whether $a_{m,k}$ falls below $\Theta_0$, above $\Theta_1$, or in between.
nodes.genus: three sets of estimates for the state of channel $m$
differentia: a_{m,k}\le \Theta_0
a_{m,k}\ge \Theta_1
\Theta_0 < a_{m,k} < \Theta_1

nodes.name: Channel classification sets $\mathcal{B}_0(t)$, $\mathcal{B}_1(t)$, $\mathcal{B}_2(t)$
nodes.statement: By the end of the sensing phase in a time slot $t$, the secondary users compute the channel availability $a_{m,k}$ for each channel $m$. During the following transmission phase, if a secondary user transmits on channel $m$, it can obtain more accurate channel state information: if its transmission is successful, then channel $m$ is idle in time slot $t$; otherwise, channel $m$ is busy in the time slot. Such channel information can be exchanged at the beginning of the sensing phase in the next time slot. Then, we can classify the $M$ channels into three sets according to the channel states in time slot $t$, including \begin{itemize} \item The set of channels that are detected or believed to be idle, denoted by $\mathcal{B}_0(t)$. \item The set of channels that are detected or believed to be busy, denoted by $\mathcal{B}_1(t)$. \item The set of channels whose states are not identified due to lack of time or not sensed by any of the secondary users, denoted by $\mathcal{B}_2(t)$. \end{itemize} Let $|\mathcal{B}_0(t)|$, $|\mathcal{B}_1(t)|$ and $|\mathcal{B}_2(t)|$ be the cardinalities of $\mathcal{B}_0(t)$, $\mathcal{B}_1(t)$, and $\mathcal{B}_2(t)$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Classify the $M$ channels in slot $t$ into believed-idle $\mathcal{B}_0(t)$, believed-busy $\mathcal{B}_1(t)$, and unidentified $\mathcal{B}_2(t)$.
nodes.genus: three sets according to the channel states in time slot $t$
differentia: The set of channels that are detected or believed to be idle
The set of channels that are detected or believed to be busy
The set of channels whose states are not identified due to lack of time or not sensed by any of the secondary users

nodes.name: Maximum tolerable collision probability $\gamma_m$
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma_m \in [0,1]$ be the maximum tolerable collision probability to primary users on channel $m$: $\gamma_m=0$ means that no secondary transmission is allowed, while $\gamma_m=1$ means that secondary users have the same privilege as primary users when accessing the channels. The probability of collision caused by secondary users to primary users should be kept below $\gamma_m$.
nodes.genus: maximum tolerable collision probability to primary users on channel $m$
differentia: $\gamma_m \in [0,1]$
$\gamma_m=0$ means that no secondary transmission is allowed
$\gamma_m=1$ means that secondary users have the same privilege as primary users when accessing the channels

nodes.name: Secondary user sensing state vector $\vec{U}$
nodes.statement: Let $\vec{U}=[U_1, U_2, \cdots, U_M]$ denote the secondary user {\em sensing state vector}, where each element $U_m$ represents the number of secondary users that choose channel $m$ to sense and access.
differentia: each element $U_m$ represents the number of secondary users that choose channel $m$ to sense and access

nodes.name: Synchronous slotted primary access with independent two-state Markov channels
nodes.statement: We assume the primary users access the channels following a synchronous slot structure as in prior work~\cite{Zhao07c, Su08JNL, Hu09}. The channel states are independent to each other and each of the $M$ channels evolves over time following a discrete-time two-state Markov process, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:ChanModel}. Such channel model has been validated by recent measurement studies~\cite{Zhao07c, Motamedi07, Su08JNL}.
nodes.statement_short: Primary users are slot-synchronous and each licensed channel evolves as an independent discrete-time two-state Markov chain.
nodes.origin_citation: Zhao & Sadler 2007; Su & Zhang 2008; Hu, Mao & Reed 2009

nodes.name: Primary user protection constraint on collision probability
nodes.statement: We assume a secondary network collocated with the $M$ primary networks, within which $N$ secondary users take advantage of the spectrum white spaces in $M$ licensed channels for data transmissions. For protection of primary users, the probability of collision caused by secondary user transmissions to primary users should be upper bounded by a prescribed threshold $\gamma_m$, for $m=1,2,\cdots,M$.
nodes.statement_short: $N$ secondary users share the $M$ licensed channels, subject to per-channel collision probability bounded by $\gamma_m$.

nodes.name: Two transceivers per secondary user: control transceiver and SDR data transceiver
nodes.statement: As in prior work~\cite{Su08JNL, Nan07, Motamedi07}, we assume that each secondary user is equipped with two transceivers: a {\em control transceiver} that operates over a dedicated control channel, which we assume is always available (e.g., a channel in the industrial, scientific and medical (ISM) band), and a {\em data transceiver} that is used for data communications through the $M$ licensed channels. The data transceiver consists of an SDR that can be tuned to any of the $M$ licensed channels to transmit and receive data. Secondary users also use their transceivers for spectrum sensing and exchanging sensing results.
nodes.statement_short: Each secondary user has an always-available control transceiver plus one SDR data transceiver used for both sensing and transmission.
nodes.origin_citation: Su & Zhang 2008; Nan, Hyon & Yoo 2007; Motamedi & Bahai 2007

nodes.name: Independence of sensing results across users and mini-slots
nodes.statement: We assume that the sensing results from different users are independent and the sensing results in different mini-slots are also independent to each other.

nodes.name: Heavy load traffic regime
nodes.statement: We consider the heavy load domain, where each secondary user always has data to send to every other secondary user.

nodes.name: Channel bonding/aggregation capability
nodes.statement: We assume that the CR users can transmit data over more than one channels using the channel bonding/aggregation techniques~\cite{Su08JNL, Corderio06}.

nodes.name: Identical sensing error probabilities across channels in simulation
nodes.statement: We assume identical false alarm probabilities $\epsilon_m = \epsilon$, and identical miss detection probabilities $\delta_m = \delta$ for all the licensed channels.

nodes.name: Steady-state busy and idle probabilities of channel $m$
nodes.statement: Let $\zeta_m = \Pr(S_m=0)$ be the probability that channel $m$ is idle (i.e., not being used by primary users). We then have \begin{eqnarray} \eta_m & = & \lim_{T\to \infty} \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T S_m(t) = \frac{1-\lambda_m}{1-\lambda_m+\mu_m} \\ \zeta_m & = & 1 - \Pr(S_m=1) = \frac{\mu_m}{1 - \lambda_m + \mu_m}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Stationary busy/idle probabilities of the two-state Markov channel in terms of $\lambda_m$ and $\mu_m$.

nodes.name: Time slot duration decomposition
nodes.statement: Let $T_s$, $T_{ms}$, and $T_{data}$ denote the duration of a time slot, a mini-slot, and the transmission phase, respectively (see Fig.~\ref{fig:SlotStructure}), we have \begin{eqnarray} T_s = \bar{K} \times T_{ms} + T_{data}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.section: 3 Sensing Error Aware CR MAC Protocol

nodes.name: Sensing error probabilities
nodes.statement: For a specific channel $m$ in a certain time slot $t$, the sensing error probabilities can be written as: \begin{eqnarray} && \Pr(W_{m,i}=1 \;|\; S_m=0)=\epsilon_m, \mbox{for all } \; i=1,2,\cdots \\ && \Pr(W_{m,i}=0 \;|\; S_m=1)=\delta_m, \mbox{for all } \; i=1,2,\cdots, \end{eqnarray} where $W_{m,i}$ is the $i$th sensing result of channel $m$ and $S_m$ is state of channel $m$.
nodes.statement_short: False alarm and miss detection expressed as conditional probabilities of the $i$th sensing result given the true channel state.

nodes.name: Binomial distribution of the number of users sensing channel $m$
nodes.statement: Let $U_m$ be the random variable representing the number of secondary users that select channel $m$ to sense. The probability that $u_m$ secondary users choose channel $m$ to sense is \begin{equation} \Pr(U_m=u_m)=\left(\!\!\! \begin{array}{c} N \\ u_m \end{array} \!\!\!\right) \left( \frac{1}{M} \right)^{u_m} \left( \frac{M-1}{M} \right)^{N-u_m}_{.} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $U_m$ is Binomial$(N,1/M)$ under uniform independent channel selection.

nodes.name: Joint distribution of the user-to-channel allocation
nodes.statement: The joint distribution that there are $u_1$ secondary users sensing channel $1$, $u_2$ secondary users sensing channel $2$, $\cdots$, and $u_M$ secondary users sensing channel $M$, is \begin{eqnarray} \Pr(u_1, u_2, \cdots, u_M) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \prod_{m=1}^M \Pr(U_m=u_m), & \mbox{if } \; \sum_{m=1}^M u_m=N \\ 0, & \mbox{otherwise}. \end{array} \right. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Joint allocation probability is the product of the marginals on the simplex summing to $N$, and zero elsewhere.

nodes.name: Conditional probability of stop time $K_m=1$ on an idle channel
nodes.statement: There are $U_m$ users sensing channel $m$ and $U_m K_m$ observations are available after mini-slot $K_m$, which is also a random variable. We first derive the conditional probability for event $K_m=1$, as \begin{eqnarray} && \Pr(K_m=1 \; | \; U_m=u \;, \;S_m=0) = \Pr(a_{m,u} \ge \Theta_1) \nonumber \\ & = & \sum_{d_m^1 \in \Psi^1_{m,u}} \left(\!\!\! \begin{array}{c} u \\ d_m^1 \end{array} \!\!\!\right)\left[ (\epsilon_m)^{u-d_m^1}(1-\epsilon_m)^{d_m^1} \right], \end{eqnarray} where $d_m^1$ is the number of observations whose sensing result is $0$ in the first mini-slot.
nodes.statement_short: Probability that $u$ users declare channel $m$ idle after a single mini-slot, summed over zero-counts in $\Psi^1_{m,u}$.

nodes.name: Conditional probability of stop time $K_m=2$ on an idle channel
nodes.statement: Following similar reasoning as in (\ref{eq:CondStop1}), we can obtain the conditional probability for the event that the stop time $K_m=2$ as \begin{eqnarray} && \Pr(K_m=2 \; | \; U_m=u \;, \;S_m=0) = \Pr \left[(\Theta_0 < a_{m,u} < \Theta_1) \cap (a_{m,2u} \ge \Theta_1) \right] \nonumber \\ & = & \hspace*{-0.1in} \sum_{D_m^2 \in \Psi^1_{m,2u}}\sum_{d_m^1 \in \Psi^2_{m,u}} \hspace*{-0.1in} \left(\!\!\! \begin{array}{c} u \\ d_m^1 \end{array} \!\!\!\right) \left(\!\!\! \begin{array}{c} u \\ d_m^2 \end{array} \!\!\!\right) \left[(\epsilon_m)^{2u-D_m^2} (1-\epsilon_m)^{D_m^2}\right], \end{eqnarray} where $\Psi^{2}_{m,k}$ is defined in (\ref{eq:Psi2}) and $D_m^2=d_m^1 + d_m^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Two-mini-slot stop probability: stay undecided after the first mini-slot, then cross the upper threshold at the second.

nodes.name: Conditional probability of general stop time $K_m=k$ on an idle channel
nodes.statement: In the general case, we can derive the conditional probability for the event that the stop time is $K_m=k$ as: \begin{eqnarray} & & \hspace*{-0.1in} \Pr(K_m=k \; | \; U_m=u\; , \; S_m=0) \nonumber \\ & & \hspace*{-0.25in} = \Pr \left[(\Theta_0 < a_{m,u} < \Theta_1)\cap (\Theta_0 < a_{m,2u} < \Theta_1) \cap \cdots \cap (\Theta_0 < a_{m,(k-1)u} < \Theta_1) \cap (a_{m,ku}\ge \Theta_1) \right] \nonumber \\ & & \hspace*{-0.25in} = \sum_{D_m^k \in \Psi^1_{m,ku}} \sum_{D_m^{k-1} \in \Psi^2_{m,(k-1)u}}\cdots \sum_{d_m^1 \in \Psi^2_{m,u}} \left(\!\!\! \begin{array}{c} u \\ d_m^1 \end{array} \!\!\!\right) \left(\!\!\! \begin{array}{c} u \\ d_m^2 \end{array} \!\!\!\right) \cdots \left(\!\!\! \begin{array}{c} u \\ d_m^k \end{array} \!\!\!\right) \left[ (\epsilon_m)^{ku-D_m^k}(1-\epsilon_m)^{D_m^k} \right], \end{eqnarray} where $k = 1, \cdots, \bar{K}$ and $D_m^k=\sum_{i=1}^k d_m^i$. We will apply these results in Section~\ref{subsec:throughput} to derive the throughput of the CR network by the {\em law of total probability}.
nodes.statement_short: General-$k$ stop-time distribution on an idle channel: undecided through mini-slot $k-1$, then above $\Theta_1$ at mini-slot $k$.

nodes.name: Case 1 per-channel access probabilities $P_m^{idle}, P_m^{succ}, P_m^{coll}$
nodes.statement: We define $P_m^{idle}$, $P_m^{succ}$ and $P_m^{coll}$ as the probability that there is no RTS transmission on channel $m$, the probability that exactly one secondary user successfully transmits an RTS on channel $m$, and the probability that there is collision on channel $m$ when multiple RTS packets are transmitted, respectively. Recall that $U_m$ is the number of secondary users that choose channel $m$ to sense. This set of secondary users also attempt to access channel $m$ if it is found idle. With $p$-persistent CSMA, it follows that \begin{eqnarray} && \hspace*{-0.4in} P_m^{idle}(U_m) = (1-p)^{U_m} \\ && \hspace*{-0.4in} P_m^{succ}(U_m) = U_m\times p\times(1-p)^{U_m-1} \\ && \hspace*{-0.4in} P_m^{coll}(U_m) = 1 - P_m^{idle}(U_m) - P_m^{succ}(U_m) = 1-(1-p)^{U_m}-U_m\times p\times(1-p)^{U_m-1}_{.} \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Idle/success/collision probabilities of $p$-persistent RTS contention among the $U_m$ users on channel $m$.

nodes.name: Case 2 control-channel access probabilities $P^{idle}, P^{succ}, P^{coll}$
nodes.statement: We define $P^{idle}$, $P^{succ}$ and $P^{coll}$ as the probability of no RTS transmission on the control channel, the probability that exactly one RTS sent on the control channel, and the probability of collision on the control channel, respectively. For $p$-Persistent CSMA, we have \begin{eqnarray} && \hspace*{-0.4in} P^{idle}(N) = (1-p)^{N} \\ && \hspace*{-0.4in} P^{succ}(N) = N\times(1-p)^{N-1} \\ && \hspace*{-0.4in} P^{coll}(N) = 1 - P^{idle}(N) - P^{succ}(N) = 1-(1-p)^{N}-N\times p \times (1-p)^{N-1}_{.} \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Idle/success/collision probabilities of $p$-persistent RTS contention among all $N$ users on the control channel.

nodes.name: Conditional probability of stop time $K_m=k$ on a busy channel (miss detection)
nodes.statement: We first derive the conditional probability that channel $m$ is miss detected to be idle by $u$ secondary users after mini-slot $k$, as follows. \begin{eqnarray} & & \hspace*{-0.2in} \Pr(K_m=k \; | \; U_m=u,S_m=1) \nonumber \\ & & \hspace*{-0.4in} = \sum_{D_m^k \in \Psi^1_{m,ku}} \sum_{D_m^{k-1} \in \Psi^2_{m,(k-1)u}}\cdots \sum_{d_m^1 \in \Psi^2_{m,u}} \left(\!\!\! \begin{array}{c} u \\ d_m^1 \end{array} \!\!\!\right) \left(\!\!\! \begin{array}{c} u \\ d_m^2 \end{array} \!\!\!\right) \cdots \left(\!\!\! \begin{array}{c} u \\ d_m^k \end{array} \!\!\!\right)(\delta_m)^{D_m^k}(1-\delta_m)^{ku-D_m^k}_{.} \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Same stop-time expansion as the idle case but with miss-detection probability $\delta_m$, giving the probability a busy channel is declared idle.

nodes.name: Case 1 interference probability $P_{m,1}^{intf}$
nodes.statement: In Case 1, the idle channels are accessed by different secondary users. The probability that secondary users collide with primary users on channel $m$ is \begin{eqnarray} P_{m,1}^{intf} = \sum_{k=1}^{\bar{K}}\sum_{u=0}^N \Pr(K_m=k \; | \; U_m=u,S_m=1) \times \Pr(U_m=u) \times \left[ P_m^{succ}(u)+P_m^{coll}(u) \right]. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Total-probability sum over stop time and user count of miss detection times any RTS transmission on channel $m$.

nodes.name: Case 2 interference probability $P_{m,2}^{intf}$
nodes.statement: In Case 2, a winning secondary user takes all the idle channels using the channel bonding/aggregation technique. The probability that secondary users collide with primary users on channel $m$ is \begin{eqnarray} P_{m,2}^{intf} = \sum_{k=1}^{\bar{K}}\sum_{u=0}^N \Pr(K_m=k \; | \; U_m=u,S_m=1) \times \Pr(U_m=u) \times P^{succ}(N). \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Same interference sum as Case 1 but weighted by the control-channel success probability of the single winning user.

nodes.name: Primary user protection constraint
nodes.statement: For primary user protection, the probability of secndary users causing collision with primary users on channel $m$ should be kept lower than or equal to $\gamma_m$, i.e., \begin{eqnarray} P_m^{intf} \le \gamma_m. \end{eqnarray} This constraint is used to set the channel access probability $p$ for the $p$-persistent CSMA protocol.
nodes.statement_short: Interference constraint $P_m^{intf}\le\gamma_m$, used to tune the access probability $p$.

nodes.name: Case 1 per-channel expected throughput $\Lambda^1_m(u)$
nodes.statement: In Case 1, the expected throughput of channel $m$ that is sensed by $u$ users, denoted by $\Lambda^1_m(u)$, can be derived as \begin{eqnarray} \Lambda^1_m(u) = \sum_{k=1}^{\bar{K}}\Pr(K_m=k\; | \; U_m=u,S_m=0) \times R_m \times \frac{1}{T_s} \times \left[ (\bar{K}-k) T_{ms} + T_{data} \right], \end{eqnarray} where $R_m$ is the data rate of channel $m$, and $T_s$ is the time slot duration given in (\ref{eq:ts}).
nodes.statement_short: Expected channel-$m$ throughput in Case 1, crediting the unused mini-slots after early sensing stop to data transmission.

nodes.name: Case 1 aggregate CR network throughput $\Omega_1$
nodes.statement: The aggregate throughput for the CR network, denoted by $\Omega_1$, is \begin{eqnarray} \Omega_1 = \sum_{\vec{U}} \Pr(\vec{U}) \sum_{\vec{S}} \Pr(\vec{S}) \sum_{m=1}^M \left( I_{[S_m=0]}\Lambda^1_m(u) \times P_m^{succ}(u) \right), \end{eqnarray} where $\vec{S}$ is the channel state vector defined in Section~\ref{sec:model}, $P_m^{succ}(u)$ is given in (\ref{eq:pmsucc}) and $I_{[S_m=0]}$ is an indicator that channel $m$ is idle, i.e., \begin{equation} I_{[S_m=0]} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & \mbox{if } S_m=0 \\ 0, & \mbox{otherwise}. \end{array} \right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Aggregate Case 1 throughput averaged over the sensing state vector $\vec{U}$ and the channel state vector $\vec{S}$.

nodes.name: Case 2 per-channel expected throughput $\Lambda^2_m(u)$
nodes.statement: We can derive the throughput for channel $m$ as follows. \begin{eqnarray} \Lambda^2_m(u) = \sum_{k=1}^{\bar{K}}\Pr(K_m=k\; | \; U_m=u,S_m=0) \times R_m \times \frac{T_{data}}{T_s}, \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Expected channel-$m$ throughput in Case 2, where transmission always starts only after all $\bar{K}$ mini-slots.

nodes.name: Case 2 aggregate CR network throughput $\Omega_2$
nodes.statement: The aggregate throughput for the CR network, denoted by $\Omega_2$, is \begin{eqnarray} \Omega_2=\sum_{\vec{U}} \Pr(\vec{U}) \sum_{\vec{S}} \Pr(\vec{S}) \sum_{m=1}^M \left( I_{[S_m=0]}\Lambda^2_m(u) P^{succ}(N) \right). \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Aggregate Case 2 throughput, weighting each idle channel by the single control-channel winner's success probability.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of $a_{m,k}$ in the number of sensing results
nodes.statement: When channel $m$ is idle, $a_{m,k}$ is a monotone increasing function of $k$; when channel $m$ is busy, $a_{m,k}$ is a monotone decreasing function of $k$.
conclusions: $a_{m,k}$ is a monotone increasing function of $k$
$a_{m,k}$ is a monotone decreasing function of $k$

nodes.name: Proof of the monotonicity of $a_{m,k}$
nodes.statement:
From the defintion of $a_{m,k}$ in (ef{eq:AvailProb}), it follows that  egin{eqnarray} &&\Pr(a_{m,k}\ge	heta_1) 
onumber \ &=&\Pr \left( \left( 1 +  rac{\eta_m}{\zeta_m} \left( rac{\delta_m}{1-\epsilon_m} ight)^{\sum_{i=1}^k ar{W}_{m,i}} \left( rac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m} ight)^{\sum_{i=1}^k W_{m,i}} ight)^{-1}\ge	heta_1 ight) 
onumber \ &=&\Pr \left( \left( rac{\delta_m}{1-\epsilon_m} ight)^{\sum_{i=1}^k ar{W}_{m,i}} \left( rac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m} ight)^{\sum_{i=1}^k W_{m,i}}\le \left( rac{1}{	heta_1}-1 ight)  rac{\zeta_m}{\eta_m} ight) 
onumber \ &=&\Pr \left( \sum_{i=1}^k \left( W_{m,i}\log \left(  rac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m} ight) -  ar{W}_{m,i} \log \left(  rac{1-\epsilon_m}{\delta_m} ight) ight) \le \chi_m ight) \end{eqnarray} where $ ar{W}_{m,i}=1-W_{m,i}$ and $\chi_m=\log(( rac{1}{	heta_1}-1) rac{\zeta_m}{\eta_m})$. Since $\epsilon_m <0.5$ and $\delta_m<0.5$ for practical sensors, both $\log \left(  rac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m} ight)$ and $\log \left(  rac{1-\epsilon_m}{\delta_m} ight)$ are positive. If $S_m(t)=0$, we have that $\Pr(W_{i,k+1}=1)<\Pr(W_{i,k+1}=0)=\Pr( ar{W}_{i,k+1}=1)$. It follows that $\Pr(a_{m,k}\ge	heta_1) < \Pr(a_{m,k+1}\ge	heta_1)$. That is, $a_{m,k}$ is a monotone increasing function of $k$. Similarly, we can show that $\Pr(a_{m,k}\le	heta_0) < \Pr(a_{m,k+1}\le	heta_0)$ when $S_m(t)=1$. That is, $a_{m,k}$ is a monotone decreasing function of $k$ when the channel is busy.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the threshold event as a log-likelihood-ratio sum, then compare mini-slot $k$ with $k+1$ separately for the idle and busy cases.

nodes.name: Reduce the threshold event to a log-likelihood-ratio sum
nodes.statement:
From the defintion of $a_{m,k}$ in (ef{eq:AvailProb}), it follows that  egin{eqnarray} &&\Pr(a_{m,k}\ge	heta_1) 
onumber \ &=&\Pr \left( \left( 1 +  rac{\eta_m}{\zeta_m} \left( rac{\delta_m}{1-\epsilon_m} ight)^{\sum_{i=1}^k ar{W}_{m,i}} \left( rac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m} ight)^{\sum_{i=1}^k W_{m,i}} ight)^{-1}\ge	heta_1 ight) 
onumber \ &=&\Pr \left( \left( rac{\delta_m}{1-\epsilon_m} ight)^{\sum_{i=1}^k ar{W}_{m,i}} \left( rac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m} ight)^{\sum_{i=1}^k W_{m,i}}\le \left( rac{1}{	heta_1}-1 ight)  rac{\zeta_m}{\eta_m} ight) 
onumber \ &=&\Pr \left( \sum_{i=1}^k \left( W_{m,i}\log \left(  rac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m} ight) -  ar{W}_{m,i} \log \left(  rac{1-\epsilon_m}{\delta_m} ight) ight) \le \chi_m ight) \end{eqnarray} where $ ar{W}_{m,i}=1-W_{m,i}$ and $\chi_m=\log(( rac{1}{	heta_1}-1) rac{\zeta_m}{\eta_m})$.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the closed form of $a_{m,k}$, invert, and take logarithms to get a sum of per-observation log terms against a constant $\chi_m$.

nodes.name: Idle case: monotone increasing
nodes.statement: Since $\epsilon_m <0.5$ and $\delta_m<0.5$ for practical sensors, both $\log \left( \frac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m} \right)$ and $\log \left( \frac{1-\epsilon_m}{\delta_m} \right)$ are positive. If $S_m(t)=0$, we have that $\Pr(W_{i,k+1}=1)<\Pr(W_{i,k+1}=0)=\Pr(\bar{W}_{i,k+1}=1)$. It follows that $\Pr(a_{m,k}\ge\theta_1) < \Pr(a_{m,k+1}\ge\theta_1)$. That is, $a_{m,k}$ is a monotone increasing function of $k$.
nodes.statement_short: With both log terms positive and a $0$ reading more likely on an idle channel, an extra mini-slot raises $\Pr(a_{m,k}\ge\theta_1)$.

nodes.name: Busy case: monotone decreasing
nodes.statement: Similarly, we can show that $\Pr(a_{m,k}\le\theta_0) < \Pr(a_{m,k+1}\le\theta_0)$ when $S_m(t)=1$. That is, $a_{m,k}$ is a monotone decreasing function of $k$ when the channel is busy.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric argument for a busy channel gives the decreasing direction.

nodes.name: Probability that a channel is sensed by nobody under memoryless sensing
nodes.statement: Under the memoryless sensing policy, some channels may not be sensed by any of the secondary users. Such an event occurs with probability $\Pr (U_m=0) = \left( \frac{M-1}{M} \right)^N $, which is sufficiently large when $M$ is large and/or the number of secondary users is close to the number of channels. Secondary users will not be able to estimate the state of a channel that nobody senses, and will neither access it in the transmission phase. Therefore, the spectrum opportunities in that channel will be wasted when such events occur.
nodes.statement_short: Memoryless sensing leaves channel $m$ unsensed with probability $((M-1)/M)^N$, wasting its spectrum opportunities.
conclusions: Such an event occurs with probability $\Pr (U_m=0) = \left( \frac{M-1}{M} \right)^N $
the spectrum opportunities in that channel will be wasted when such events occur

nodes.name: CR MAC design problem: capacity versus primary user protection
nodes.statement: One of the main challenges in designing a CR network MAC protocol is how to balance the tension between maximizing the capacity of secondary users and protecting primary users from harmful collisions.
nodes.statement_short: Design a CR MAC that maximizes secondary user capacity subject to bounded collision with primary users.

nodes.name: Threshold-based channel sensing decision rule
nodes.statement: During the sensing phase, each secondary user chooses one channel to sense with equal probability at the beginning of the time slot. Secondary users also report their sensing results over the control channel, and share the corresponding channel sensing results during the mini-slots. Two threshold probabilities $\Theta_0 < \Theta_1$ are used for decision making. \begin{itemize} \item If the availability of channel $m$, i.e., $a_{m,k}$, is below $\Theta_0$, the channel is believed to be busy and the secondary users will wait till the next time slot to start sensing again. \item If the availability of channel $m$ is between $\Theta_0$ and $\Theta_1$, secondary users will keep on sensing the same channel to obtain more sensing results for more accurate estimation of the channel state, until the maximum number of mini-slots, $\bar{K}$, is reached. \item If the availability of channel $m$ exceeds $\Theta_1$, the channel is believed to be idle and the secondary users stop sensing and prepare to access the channel (see Section~\ref{subsec:transph}). \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Sequential two-threshold test on $a_{m,k}$: declare busy below $\Theta_0$, keep sensing in between, declare idle above $\Theta_1$.
output: the channel is believed to be busy
the channel is believed to be idle and the secondary users stop sensing and prepare to access the channel

nodes.name: Declare busy below the lower threshold
nodes.statement: If the availability of channel $m$, i.e., $a_{m,k}$, is below $\Theta_0$, the channel is believed to be busy and the secondary users will wait till the next time slot to start sensing again.
nodes.statement_short: Below $\Theta_0$: declare busy and back off to the next time slot.

nodes.name: Continue sensing in the undecided region
nodes.statement: If the availability of channel $m$ is between $\Theta_0$ and $\Theta_1$, secondary users will keep on sensing the same channel to obtain more sensing results for more accurate estimation of the channel state, until the maximum number of mini-slots, $\bar{K}$, is reached.
nodes.statement_short: Between the thresholds: keep sensing the same channel up to $\bar{K}$ mini-slots.

nodes.name: Declare idle above the upper threshold
nodes.statement: If the availability of channel $m$ exceeds $\Theta_1$, the channel is believed to be idle and the secondary users stop sensing and prepare to access the channel (see Section~\ref{subsec:transph}).
nodes.statement_short: Above $\Theta_1$: declare idle, stop sensing, and prepare to access.

nodes.name: Memoryless sensing policy
nodes.statement: We first propose a memoryless sensing policy in this section, with which secondary users cooperatively sense the licensed channels. We call the policy ``memoryless'' since it does not consider the channel sensing and access results in the previous time slot for simplicity. With this memoryless policy, each secondary user chooses one of the $M$ licensed channels to sense with equal probability, i.e., $1/M$. Furthermore, channel selections of the $N$ secondary users are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.).
nodes.statement_short: Each secondary user independently picks one of the $M$ channels uniformly at random each slot, ignoring past slots.
output: channel selections of the $N$ secondary users are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.)

nodes.name: Improved sensing policy
nodes.statement: If channel $m$ is in set $\mathcal{B}_0(t)$ and the stop time on channel $m$ is less than the maximum stop time $\bar{K}$, one user among those $u_m$ users that are sensing this channel will be randomly chosen to switch to sense another channel in the set $m \cup \mathcal{B}_1(t) \cup \mathcal{B}_2(t)$ in time slot $(t+1)$. If channel $m$ is in set $\mathcal{B}_1(t)$ and the stop time on channel $m$ is less than the maximum stop time $\bar{K}$, the secondary users that are sensing this channel will randomly choose a channel in $m \cup \mathcal{B}_2(t)$ to sense in time slot $(t+1)$. With the above mechanism that reassigns secondary users to channels based on the sensing results in the previous time slot, we can reduce the chance that a licensed channel is not sensed by any of the users. This approach achieves the {\em load balancing} effect since it attempts to spread out secondary users to the channels.
nodes.statement_short: Reassign sensing users away from already-decided channels toward busy or unidentified ones, spreading users out across channels.
output: reassigns secondary users to channels based on the sensing results in the previous time slot

nodes.name: Move one user off a believed-idle channel
nodes.statement: If channel $m$ is in set $\mathcal{B}_0(t)$ and the stop time on channel $m$ is less than the maximum stop time $\bar{K}$, one user among those $u_m$ users that are sensing this channel will be randomly chosen to switch to sense another channel in the set $m \cup \mathcal{B}_1(t) \cup \mathcal{B}_2(t)$ in time slot $(t+1)$.
nodes.statement_short: On a believed-idle channel decided early, migrate one randomly chosen sensing user elsewhere.

nodes.name: Move all users off a believed-busy channel
nodes.statement: If channel $m$ is in set $\mathcal{B}_1(t)$ and the stop time on channel $m$ is less than the maximum stop time $\bar{K}$, the secondary users that are sensing this channel will randomly choose a channel in $m \cup \mathcal{B}_2(t)$ to sense in time slot $(t+1)$.
nodes.statement_short: On a believed-busy channel decided early, let its sensing users re-pick among that channel and the unidentified ones.

nodes.name: $p$-persistent CSMA
nodes.statement: We adopt the $p$-persistent CSMA protocol for data channel access for secondary users during the data transmission phase. Under this protocol, a secondary user delays its transmission when the channels are busy. Once one or more channels are detected idle, the secondary user will attempt to access the idle channel(s) for data transmission with probability $p$.
nodes.statement_short: Contention protocol in which a user attempts transmission on a detected-idle channel with probability $p$.
input: one or more channels are detected idle
output: the secondary user will attempt to access the idle channel(s) for data transmission with probability $p$
nodes.origin_citation: $p$-persistent CSMA (classical random access protocol, adopted here)

nodes.name: Case 1 channel access: per-channel RTS contention
nodes.statement: Once the estimate of channel $m$, i.e., $a_{m,k}$, exceeds threshold $\Theta_1$, each of the secondary users sensing channel $m$ will send an RTS packet on channel $m$ with probability $p$, to contend for the transmission opportunity on this channel. If there is only one secondary user that sends RTS, then it wins the channel; if there is no secondary user that sends RTS, then the channel will not be accessed and will be wasted; if there are more than one RTS packets sent on channel $m$, there is collision and none of the secondary users can use the channel.
nodes.statement_short: Users that sensed a channel idle contend for it independently on that channel with probability $p$; exactly one RTS wins.
output: If there is only one secondary user that sends RTS, then it wins the channel
if there are more than one RTS packets sent on channel $m$, there is collision and none of the secondary users can use the channel

nodes.name: Send RTS with probability $p$ on the sensed channel
nodes.statement: Once the estimate of channel $m$, i.e., $a_{m,k}$, exceeds threshold $\Theta_1$, each of the secondary users sensing channel $m$ will send an RTS packet on channel $m$ with probability $p$, to contend for the transmission opportunity on this channel.
nodes.statement_short: Each user that declared channel $m$ idle transmits an RTS on it with probability $p$.

nodes.name: Resolve the per-channel contention outcome
nodes.statement: If there is only one secondary user that sends RTS, then it wins the channel; if there is no secondary user that sends RTS, then the channel will not be accessed and will be wasted; if there are more than one RTS packets sent on channel $m$, there is collision and none of the secondary users can use the channel.
nodes.statement_short: Exactly one RTS wins, zero wastes the channel, and two or more collide.

nodes.name: Case 2 channel access: control-channel contention with channel bonding
nodes.statement: In this case, every secondary user keeps on sensing the channel until the channel state is identified or until the end of the sensing phase. At the beginning of the transmission phase, the set of idle channels are identified and are know to all the secondary users. Then every secondary user will transmit an RTS packet with probability $p$ on the control channel, to contend for the entire set of idle channels. If there is only one secondary user that sends RTS on the control channel, it wins the entire set of idle channels. Otherwise, the idle channels will be wasted (i.e., when no RTS is sent, or more than one RTS are sent on the control channel).
nodes.statement_short: All users contend once on the control channel with probability $p$, and the single winner takes every idle channel by bonding.
input: the set of idle channels are identified and are know to all the secondary users
output: it wins the entire set of idle channels
Otherwise, the idle channels will be wasted

nodes.name: Sense until the channel state is identified
nodes.statement: In this case, every secondary user keeps on sensing the channel until the channel state is identified or until the end of the sensing phase.
nodes.statement_short: No early stop: sense until decided or until the sensing phase ends.

nodes.name: Contend on the control channel for the whole idle set
nodes.statement: At the beginning of the transmission phase, the set of idle channels are identified and are know to all the secondary users. Then every secondary user will transmit an RTS packet with probability $p$ on the control channel, to contend for the entire set of idle channels.
nodes.statement_short: Every user sends an RTS on the control channel with probability $p$ to bid for all idle channels at once.

nodes.name: Award the whole idle set to a single winner
nodes.statement: If there is only one secondary user that sends RTS on the control channel, it wins the entire set of idle channels. Otherwise, the idle channels will be wasted (i.e., when no RTS is sent, or more than one RTS are sent on the control channel).
nodes.statement_short: A lone RTS wins all idle channels; otherwise all of them go unused.

nodes.name: Random sensing scheme
nodes.statement: A simple random sensing scheme that each user chooses one channel to sense with equal probability, termed {\em Random} in the plots.
nodes.statement_short: Baseline in which each user picks a channel to sense uniformly at random.
nodes.origin_citation: simple random sensing baseline (no citation given in the paper)

nodes.name: Negotiation-based sensing policy (NSP)
nodes.statement: In a recent work~\cite{Su08JNL}, Su and Zhang propose a negotiation-based sensing policy (NSP), in which a secondary user knows which channels are already sensed and will choose a different channel to sense.
nodes.statement_short: Baseline policy where users negotiate to sense distinct channels.
output: will choose a different channel to sense

nodes.name: Two implications of an early stop time
nodes.statement: We next derive the conditional probability that secondary users compete for the channel after the sensing phase stops at the end of mini-slot $K_m < \bar{K}$. The stop time $K_m < \bar{K}$ has two implications. First, it means that secondary users stop sensing channel $m$ after mini-slot $K_m$. Second, it indicates that the estimated availability of channel $m$, $a_{m,k}$, has already exceeded the threshold $\Theta_1$. Thus these secondary users think channel $m$ is idle and are ready to access the channel for data transmission. Note that a secondary user also stops sensing a channel $m$ when $a_{m,k} < \Theta_0$ (when it is sure that the channel is busy). We are not interested in this case, since the secondary user will back off until the next time slot. Thus $K_m$ is defined with regard to the event $a_{m,k} > \Theta_1$.
nodes.statement_short: $K_m$ is defined only with respect to crossing the upper threshold, since a below-$\Theta_0$ stop leads to back-off rather than access.

nodes.name: Abuse of notation for pooled sensing results
nodes.statement: For the secondary user, it is also possible that it obtains some of the $k$ sensing results by local measurements, and receives the remaining sensing results from the control channel in the case that some other secondary users are sensing the same channel $m$. By abuse of notation, we also use $a_{m,k}$ to denote the conditional channel availability probability in this case, due to independence of the sensing results.
nodes.statement_short: By independence, $a_{m,k}$ also covers $k$ results pooled from several users, not only $k$ local mini-slots.

nodes.name: Early stopping in Case 1 versus fixed sensing phase in Case 2
nodes.statement: In Case 1, the sensing process on channel $m$ can stop early if the estimate of channel availability $a_{m,k}$ exceeds threshold $\Theta_1$ or drops below the threshold $\Theta_0$. In the former case, the remaining mini-slots can be used to transmit data. In Case 2, all CR users wait till the beginning of the transmission phase, and then contend for the idle channels by sending RTS packets on the control channel. The winning secondary user's data transmissions start at the beginning of the transmission phase (i.e., after $\bar{K}$ mini-slots).
nodes.statement_short: Case 1 can reclaim leftover mini-slots for data; Case 2 always transmits only after all $\bar{K}$ mini-slots.

nodes.name: Approximation underlying the improved sensing analysis
nodes.statement: The gap is actually due to an approximation we used for the secondary user sensing state vector $\vec{U}$, for which deriving the exact form is non-trivial. In the analysis, we assume that the probability is 0 that a channel is not sensed by any secondary user. We find the analysis can serve as a tight upper bound for the CR MAC throughput performance when the improved sensing policy is incorporated.
nodes.statement_short: The improved-policy analysis assumes no channel is left unsensed, making it a tight upper bound rather than exact.

nodes.name: Prior work assumes perfect channel sensing
nodes.statement: Many prior works~\cite{Le08, Su08JNL, Jia08JNL, Motamedi07} assume perfect channel sensing, within which secondary users can always sense the channel correctly. Sensing errors are not considered.

nodes.name: Separation principle for opportunistic spectrum access under sensing errors
nodes.statement: The joint design of opportunistic spectrum access and sensing policies is studied in a recent work~\cite{YChen08} in the presence of sensing errors. The authors develop a separation principle that decouples the designs of sensing and access policy. This interesting study is based on a constrained partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) formulation and thus has an exponentially growing computational complexity~\cite{YChen08}.
nodes.statement_short: A cited POMDP-based separation principle decouples sensing and access design but is exponentially expensive.

nodes.name: Motivation for the improved sensing policy
nodes.statement: Motivated by this observation, we develop an {\em improved sensing} policy that attempts to reduce the chance that a channel is not sensed by any of the secondary users. The improved sensing policy incorporates a mechanism to spread secondary users to the channels. It also exploits channel state autocorrelation by considering sensing results and channel states in the previous time slot.
nodes.statement_short: The improved policy spreads users across channels and exploits channel autocorrelation from the previous slot.

nodes.name: Rationale for comparing against negotiate sensing
nodes.statement: We choose the negotiate sensing scheme since it adopts a similar network model and assumptions. With this scheme, different secondary users attempt to select distinct channels to sense by overhearing the control packets on the control channel~\cite{Su08JNL}. One of the major differences between negotiate sensing and the proposed schemes in this paper, is that negotiate sensing does not consider spectrum sensing errors in the MAC protocol design.
nodes.statement_short: Negotiate sensing is the natural baseline: same network model, but no sensing-error awareness.

nodes.name: Verification of the throughput analysis against simulation
nodes.statement: We first verify our throughput analysis presented in Section~\ref{sec:crmac}. In Figs~\ref{fig:FalseAlarmRes} and~\ref{fig:MissDetecRes}, we plot the throughputs for the CR MACs incorporating the memoryless sensing policy and the improved sensing policy, with both simulation and analysis curves (dashed curves). We observe that the simulation and analysis curves for the memoryless sensing CR MACs overlap completely with each other, indicating that our analysis is exact. Furthermore, although there is a gap between the simulation and analysis curves for the CR MACs with the improved sensing policy, the gap is generally very small.
nodes.statement_short: Simulation matches the memoryless analysis exactly and the improved-policy analysis closely.

nodes.name: Throughput versus false alarm probability
nodes.statement: In Fig.~\ref{fig:FalseAlarmRes}, we plot the throughputs obtained by the four schemes versus the false alarm probability $\epsilon$. Specifically, we fix $\delta$ at 0.3 and increase $\epsilon$ from $0.1$ to $0.5$. Intuitively, a higher false alarm probability results in lower probability for secondary users to exploit the transmission opportunities in the licensed channels. This is illustrated in the figure, as all the four throughput curves decrease as $\epsilon$ is increased. The improved sensing MAC achieves the best performance, with about 10\% gain over the memoryless sensing MAC and about 200\% gain over the two existing approaches. The advantage of channel bonding/aggregation is also demonstrated in the figure, where Case 2 transmission scheme always achieves higher throughput than Case 1 scheme.
nodes.statement_short: All schemes lose throughput as $\epsilon$ grows; improved sensing leads, and Case 2 beats Case 1.

nodes.name: Throughput versus miss detection probability
nodes.statement: In Fig.~\ref{fig:MissDetecRes}, we examine the impact of miss detection probability  $\delta$ on the CR network throughput. In these simulations, we fix $\epsilon$ at 0.3 and increase $\delta$ from $0.1$ to $0.5$. We find that the miss detection error has small impact on the throughputs of the random sensing and negotiate sensing protocols, since miss detection errors are not considered in the design of these protocols. However, both our proposed CR MAC schemes achieve considerable throughput gains over the random sensing and negotiate sensing schemes.
nodes.statement_short: Sweeping $\delta$ barely moves the baselines but the proposed schemes still dominate.

nodes.name: Throughput versus channel utilization with idle-probability upper bound
nodes.statement: In Fig.~\ref{fig:UtilityRes}, we plot the throughput of the four schemes under different channel utilization values ranging from $0.3$ to $0.7$. As utilization of the licensed channels is increased, the transmission opportunities for secondary users are clearly reduced. Therefore the four curves are all decreasing function of $\eta$. The improved policy with transmission scheme Case 2 achieves the best performance among the four schemes, while random sensing has the poorest performance. When the channel utilization is $\eta=0.3$, the improved policy achieves a $10\%$ gain in throughput over the memoryless sensing policy. We also plot the upper bound on the CR network throughput, as given by the channel idle probability in (\ref{eq:ProbIdle}). When the channel utilization is low, the improved policy with transmission scheme Case 2 can achieve a throughput very close to the upper bound. The gap between the upper bound and the achievable throughput increase when the primary users get more busy.
nodes.statement_short: Throughput falls with $\eta$; improved sensing with Case 2 approaches the channel-idle-probability upper bound at low utilization.

nodes.name: Collision probability with primary users under a 3.5\% budget
nodes.statement: In Fig.~\ref{fig:collision}, we plot the collision probability caused by secondary transmissions to primary users, when the maximum allowable collision probability is set as $\gamma=3.5\%$. We plot the measured collision probabilities in the simulations when the channel utilization is increased from 30\% to 70\%. It can be seen that the collision probabilities of random and negotiate sensing schemes increases along with $\eta$ and soon exceed the 3.5\% threshold. On the other hand, the collision probabilities of the proposed schemes are kept around 2.5\% for the entire range of $\eta$ examined.
nodes.statement_short: The proposed schemes hold collisions near 2.5\% across $\eta$ while the baselines breach the 3.5\% budget.

nodes.name: Primary user throughput under the four schemes
nodes.statement: Finally, we plot the throughput of the primary users in Fig.~\ref{fig:primarythput}. The primary user throughput curves for all the four schemes increase when the channel utilization $\eta$ is increased. The gap between the curves of the proposed schemes and those of random and negotiate sensing schemes, is due to the different collision rates secondary users introduce to primary users under these schemes (see Fig.~\ref{fig:collision}). As $\eta$ is increased, the proposed schemes introduces relatively constant collision rates to primary users (i.e., around 2.5\%), while the random and negotiate sensing schemes introduce increasingly higher collision rates to primary users, which degrade the throughput of primary users.
nodes.statement_short: Primary throughput is higher under the proposed schemes because their collision rate stays flat as utilization grows.
